Source File [231.4 MB ] Preview file [ ] Credits ESA [ Science ] BepiColombo entering orbit around Mercury 19 NOV. 2026 publication date 1517 Views Science BepiColombo Details Videos: Digital Title: BepiColombo entering orbit around Mercury Released: 19/11/2026 Length: 00:00:38 Language: English Media type: Animation Format: Horizontal Camera shot type: Close-up, Exterior Shot, Medium Shot This animation shows the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission entering orbit around Mercury in November 2026. The stacked spacecraft is made up of the European Space Agency’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter ( MPO ) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Mio orbiter, with the latter sheltered within a sunshield. Four of MPO’s thrusters fire to carefully slow down the spacecraft as it approaches Mercury’s south pole, ensuring that the spacecraft stack gets captured into orbit around the small, rocky planet. BepiColombo approaches on Mercury’s night side and will initially enter an elliptical 590 x 11 640 km orbit. This orbit insertion is one step of many for BepiColombo’s arrival at Mercury. After this, MPO and Mio will separate from each other on 9–10 December 2026, after which point BepiColombo will be the first mission flying two spacecraft around Mercury. MPO will perform many more burns in the coming months to reach its final science orbit by March 2027. Science operations for both spacecraft are set to begin in April 2027. esa_timeline.text: Media modal copy url 0 favorites publication date 0 Views News - Media Multimedia Images BepiColombo arrival at Mercury timeline … Image Source File [ 994.6 KB ] Preview file [ ] More information Credits Related links Related images Copy url Share this content Social media platforms Messaging direct share [ Science ] BepiColombo arrival at Mercury timeline 10 JUL. 2026 publication date 8735 Views Science BepiColombo After an eight-year journey through the inner Solar System, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission will arrive at Mercury in late 2026. This arrival happens in stages, because ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio) are travelling to Mercury as a single composite spacecraft. They are stacked on top of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM), providing power and propulsion, and Mio is sheltered within a sunshield (MOSIF). After separating, MPO and Mio go through extensive spacecraft & instrument commissioning before the science phase of the mission can begin. Key arrival stages are listed below: 3 September 2026: While still on the approach to Mercury, MTM separates from the rest. Steering is taken over by MPO's thrusters. 21 November 2026: MPO and Mio, still stacked on top of each other, are captured into a polar orbit around the planet. 9–10 December 2026: MPO releases Mio onto her final elliptical polar orbit. 16 December 2026: MPO releases Mio's sunshield (MOSIF), and descends to its own orbit using its thrusters. 10 March 2027: MPO arrives in its final orbit. 6 April 2027: The science phase of the mission begins. Note: Exact dates may change for operational reasons. This graphic and its caption were updated in July 2026. [Image description: An infographic showing the different stages of BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury. Each step shows the configuration of the different spacecraft as they separate from one another, depicted as simplified grey drawings on a dark blue background. A vertical line connects the image for each step to the corresponding date and description at the bottom. warwick.text: First women join world’s largest AI assisted breast screening trial Hundreds of women are now being invited to the Warwick-led EDITH trial, the world’s largest artificial intelligence (AI) assisted breast screening trial, which could transform breast cancer diagnosis. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, with around 55,000 cases diagnosed in the UK every year. Around 2.2 million women in the UK have breast screening each year, and all women aged 50 to 71 are invited every three years. Over the next three years, nearly 700,000 women attending routine NHS breast screening will be invited to take part in the EDITH trial , which will test whether AI-assisted tools can improve early cancer detection and enabling specialist clinicians to spend more time supporting people with cancer. The £10m EDITH trial is funded through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and co-led by Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips at the University of Warwick and Professor Fiona Gilbert at the University of Cambridge and Addenbrooke’s Hospital, working closely with NHS England. Recruitment has started at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK, with further sites opening in the coming months and thousands more women set to be invited. Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips, NIHR Research Professor and Professor of Population Health at the University of Warwick, and Chief Investigator of the EDITH trial said: "EDITH will test whether AI can help NHS staff improve the service for women attending the NHS Breast Screening Programme. AI-assisted technology could support staff by flagging areas of a mammogram where cancer might be missed to improve early cancer detection." "We have rigorously tested four AI systems for accuracy and will use these safely and transparently. Importantly, all clinical decisions during EDITH will remain with NHS staff. "Now the trial is underway, we can find out whether these benefits can be delivered across 30 NHS sites in the UK.” Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper visited the trial team at the first site to begin recruiting to see the study under way. Speaking on a visit to the trial team at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, the Health and Social Care Secretary, Yvette Cooper, said: “This is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world, backed by £10 million of government investment to speed up diagnosis and potentially deliver life-saving improvements. “If successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery. “AI has huge potential, but we also need proper safeguards in place to make sure we’re using it safely and effectively to improve treatment and research. “Our National Cancer Plan is about improving diagnosis and treatment and, harnessing the world-leading research that we have in our NHS and life sciences sector to drive forward world-beating treatments for cancer.” Women will be invited for screening as usual, but their invitation letter will include details of the trial and how to opt-out for anyone who does not want to take part. Currently, each mammogram is reviewed by two specialist radiologists. Fewer than 1% show signs of cancer, so significant time is spent reviewing negative images. The AI tool will be used to help review images collected from routine mammograms, which are designed to find cancers that are too small to see or feel. The trial will explore whether it could safely support radiologists, which could mean many mammograms only need to be reviewed by one radiologist rather than two. Nothing will change during a woman’s breast screening appointment, as the trial only affects how the collected images are reviewed. Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one human radiologist, and the NHS will only change how screening works if the evidence shows it is as safe and effective as the care women receive now. Professor Fiona Gilbert, Department of Radiology, University of Cambridge and Honorary Consultant at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, and EDITH co-chief investigator said: "Millions of women have a mammogram each year and only a small number, less than 1%, will have cancer. Technology can make reviewing these images more efficient, freeing up specialist breast radiologists to spend more time caring for patients with cancer, supporting faster diagnosis and earlier treatment." cuh.text: Women invited for NHS breast screening in Cambridgeshire are the first to take part in a landmark national trial using artificial intelligence to support specialist clinicians and help detect breast cancers earlier. Nearly 700,000 women will take part in the trial. The £10 million NIHR-funded trial is the largest in the world to use an artificial intelligence-assisted tool in breast cancer screening. Cambridgeshire is the first location to launch the trial, which will soon be running at 30 breast screening sites across the UK. All women aged 50-71 are invited for screening every three years. Currently around 2.1 million women in the UK have breast screening each year, which helps prevent around 1,300 deaths. More information for women taking part in the trial is available on the EDITH patient information webpage . Shirley was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2025 Shirley, aged 70 from Cambridgeshire, was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer in October 2025 after a routine screening appointment. Following surgery and radiotherapy treatment, she is now doing well. Shirley is not part of the trial but is passionate about the importance of screening. I feel so lucky my cancer was detected early. When I received the invitation to attend, I had no symptoms and no clue anything was wrong. My routine mammogram saved my life, so anything that helps other people get diagnosed earlier is crucial. That's why this trial is so important. Reviewing breast screening x-rays (mammograms) is time intensive. Currently, each mammogram is reviewed by two specialist radiologists. Fewer than 1% of mammograms show signs of cancer, so significant time is spent reviewing negative screening images. In the trial, known as EDITH, the AI-assisted tool will be used alongside specialists checking the images to look for cancers that are too small to see or feel. This could mean many mammograms would only need to be reviewed by one radiologist and would free-up radiologists to spend more time on diagnosis and caring for women with cancer. Millions of women have a mammogram each year, and fewer than one in 100 will be diagnosed with cancer. EDITH will test whether an AI-assisted mammogram-reading tool can help experts review images more efficiently, while maintaining professional oversight and the standards women expect from NHS breast screening. Professor Fiona Gilbert, Department of Radiology, University of Cambridge and Honorary Consultant at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Watch patient Shirley and Professor Fiona Gilbert speaking about the trial Watch patient Shirley and Professor Fiona Gilbert speaking about the trial Link: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/VXB5NQvquaM The NHS offers mammograms at local breast screening clinics in GP practices or hospitals, or women can attend one of their local mobile screening vans, conveniently located in supermarket or community car parks. The trial will not change what happens during a woman’s breast screening appointment. It only affects how the collected images may be reviewed. Every mammogram will still be reviewed by at least one human radiologist. To mark the opening of the trial, the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, Yvette Cooper, visited the Breast Unit at Addenbrooke’s Hospital to meet with Shirley and the leaders of the trial, Professor Fiona Gilbert from the University of Cambridge and Addenbrooke’s Hospital and Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips at the University of Warwick. From left to right: Professor Fiona Gilbert, Yvette Cooper MP, Professor Sian Taylor-Phillips, CUH Chief Executive Nicola Ayton This is the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world, backed by £10 million of government investment to speed up diagnosis and potentially deliver life-saving improvements. If successful, this technology could help women get a breast cancer diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, giving them the best possible chance of recovery. esa_bepi_news_redirect.text: Media invitation: briefing on BepiColombo arrival at Mercury on 27 November Journalists are invited to register for a hybrid media briefing on the BepiColombo mission to Mercury to be held on Friday 27th November at 09:30GMT/10:30CET online and at the Science Museum in London. Experts from the European Space Agency (ESA), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and industrial experts from Airbus will update media on the status of the mission and the road ahead. 18 NOV. 2026 publication date Journalists are invited to register for a hybrid media briefing on the BepiColombo mission to Mercury to be held on Friday 27th November at 09:30GMT/10:30CET online and at the Science Museum in London. Experts from the European Space Agency (ESA), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and industrial experts from Airbus will update media on the status of the mission and the road ahead. After eight years of travelling through the inner Solar System, BepiColombo is arriving at Mercury. BepiColombo is a world-class science mission led by ESA in close collaboration with JAXA . It will be the first mission to orbit Mercury with two spacecraft, with ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter ( MPO ) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter ( Mio ) orbiting the planet at the same time. The arrival phase began with the successful separation of the Mercury Transfer Module ( MTM ) from the spacecraft stack on 3 September 2026. The composite spacecraft will enter orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026, and MPO and Mio will separate from each other on 9–10 December 2026. The mission’s science phase is set to begin in April 2027. To mark this occasion, and to share all details of the recent achievements and the road ahead, a hybrid media briefing will be held. The programme is: 09:30-11:00 GMT BepiColombo media briefing (onsite and online), Smith Centre Prof. Carole Mundell, ESA Science Director Prof. Masaki Fujimoto, Director General of JAXA Prof. Geraint Jones, ESA Project Scientist Assoc. Prof. Go Murakami, JAXA Project Scientist Ignacio Tanco, ESA Head of Inner Solar System Mission Operations Santa Martínez, ESA BepiColombo Mission Manager Libby Jackson, Head of Space, Science Museum (moderator) 11:00-11:30 GMT UK media session (onsite and online), Smith Centre Dr Caroline Harper, Head of Space Science at the UK Space Agency Prof. Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator for MIXS Instrument (Uni of Leicester) Justin Byrne, Head of Space Exploration at Airbus -
